title: Nothing before the work of God (ch. 43)
word: Nothing before the work of God
hookLine: when the bell rings, leave everything and go

lines: A HOE, A BOOK, A SINK.
cards: A monk is in the garden with a hoe, halfway down a row of beans. Another is in the library, one page from the end of a chapter. A third has his arms in a sink of hot water.
Then the bell rings. Not a reminder on a phone that can be snoozed. The bell.
Saint Benedict's Rule says each of them sets down whatever is in his hands, right then, and goes. The beans can wait. The dishes can definitely wait.

teach.h: THE HOURS ARE THE WORK OF GOD.
teach.b: Benedict's word for the hours of prayer is the work of God. Some readers hear in it more than the monks' work for God: God's own work, which they join.

teach.h: AT THE SIGNAL, LEAVE IT AND HURRY.
teach.b: Chapter forty-three says that at the hour of the Office, as soon as the signal is heard, the monks leave whatever they're doing and hurry.
Then a small, careful brake: hurry, but with seriousness, so nobody turns the dash to chapel into a joke. Then the line: let nothing be put before the work of God.
In chapter five, a monk left his work for a word from the abbot. Here it's a bell, and the reason is prayer itself. It's a claim about what a day is for.
The garden, the books, the dishes all matter. They just don't come first. What makes the chapter lovely is how human the rest of it is.
Benedict knows some monks will be late.

teach.h: THE PSALM GOES SLOWLY FOR LATECOMERS.
teach.b: So for the night office, the opening psalm is said slowly, drawn out, to give latecomers time to arrive.
Someone who comes after it ends doesn't stay outside, either, where Benedict worries he might go back to sleep, or sit by the door chatting.
He comes in and stands in a separate place, a little embarrassed, but inside.

teach.h: LET NOTHING BE PUT BEFORE THE WORK OF GOD.
teach.b: The bar is high, and the door stays open. Without a monastery bell, the question is the same: when something is ringing for prayer, what gets set down, and what waits?

how: In Benedictine monasteries a bell calls the community to the hours, and monks and nuns leave their work to gather in choir; some Catholics outside monasteries pause at set times, such as the Angelus at noon.

games.q: what does “nothing before the work of god” mean?
o: a rule that monks finish all work before praying
the idea that farm work matters more than study
Benedict's rule that prayer comes before every task

p: Benedict's name for the hours of prayer

s: Benedict tells monks to run to chapel as fast as they can, any way they can
hurry, he says, but with seriousness, so it never turns into a joke.
the night office's opening psalm is drawn out so latecomers can arrive
Benedict asks for it to be said slowly for that reason.
in the Rule, a late monk must wait outside the chapel
he comes in and stands apart; left outside, he might go back to sleep or chat.

games.q: you're a monk who overslept. the night office has already begun when you reach the chapel door. what does the Rule ask?
o: stay outside so you don't disturb anyone.
come in and stand in a separate place.
go back to bed and come to the next hour.
games.why: Benedict wants latecomers inside, standing apart, rather than outside, where they might sleep or chat.

practice: Let your mind start on something, planning dinner, a list for tomorrow, a message you need to send, and get halfway in.

Then stop without finishing the thought; set it down the way a monk sets down a hoe, and turn toward God, or simply toward the quiet, for a few breaths, noticing how hard it is to leave a thing unfinished.
If you pray, use any short prayer you already know.

wordCard.voice: Nothing before the work of God. Benedict's rule for the bell: when it's time to pray, everything else waits. Today's word.

orig.note: Latin, the line from chapter forty-three: let nothing be put before the work of God.

carryVoice: Your line: nothing before prayer. The beans and the dishes will still be there afterward. Rest well.
